name: Reading Comprehension
blurb: Read faster, map arguments, and recognize trap types, with checkpoint exams that confirm each group before you move on.

nodes.title: Start Here
nodes.description: Take one timed short passage and note where you lose time or accuracy. Clear this node to open the first group of topics.
nodes.tip: Time the passage, then classify each miss as a detail, inference, or trap answer.

nodes.title: Main Idea & Theme
nodes.description: Distinguish topic, main idea, and theme across paragraphs and whole passages.
nodes.tip: State the passage's point in one sentence before looking at the choices.

nodes.title: Supporting Details
nodes.description: Locate explicit evidence and distinguish it from plausible but unsupported claims.
nodes.tip: Every detail answer must be provable by a specific line; no line, no selection.

nodes.title: Vocabulary in Context
nodes.description: Infer word meaning from syntax, contrast, and examples inside the passage.
nodes.tip: Cover the word and predict a substitute from the sentence, then match your prediction to the options.

nodes.title: Inference & Implication
nodes.description: Draw only the conclusions the text forces, not ones that are merely possible.
nodes.tip: Ask 'does the passage have to mean this?' If not, eliminate the choice.

nodes.title: Text Structure & Organization
nodes.description: Chronology, cause and effect, comparison, problem-solution, and their signposts.
nodes.tip: Map the passage's skeleton (each paragraph's purpose) rather than its content.

nodes.title: Active Reading & Annotation
nodes.description: Read with purpose: mark claims, turns, and names instead of highlighting everything.
nodes.tip: Annotate the margin with two or three words per paragraph; it makes questions locatable.

nodes.title: Question-Type Strategy
nodes.description: Match question stems to the right reading approach and predicted answer.
nodes.tip: Read the question stem before the answer choices; predicting first prevents trap answers.

nodes.title: Skimming for Gist
nodes.description: Preview a passage quickly by reading the first and last sentences of each paragraph.
nodes.tip: Spend 20 seconds previewing the structure before you read closely; it reduces re-reading.

nodes.title: Comprehension Exam
nodes.description: Checkpoint covering main idea, supporting details, vocabulary in context, inference, text structure, active reading, question types, and skimming.
nodes.tip: Score 80% or higher to master this checkpoint and unlock the next group.

questions.prompt:
Passage: Urban gardens turn empty lots into shared green spaces. They grow food, cool the surrounding streets, and give neighbours a place to meet.

Which sentence best states the main idea?
choices: Urban gardens provide food, cooling, and community benefits.
Empty lots are always better as gardens.
Urban gardens are mainly a source of profit.
questions.explanation: The passage lists several benefits of urban gardens: food, cooling, and community space. The other choices are either extreme or unsupported.

questions.prompt: Using the same passage, which detail is explicitly stated?
choices: Urban gardens cool the surrounding streets.
Urban gardens exist only in Manila.
questions.explanation: The passage directly says gardens 'cool the surrounding streets.' The other details are not stated.

questions.prompt:
The garden's harvest was sparse, yielding only a few baskets of vegetables.

What does 'sparse' most nearly mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'only a few baskets' shows that sparse means scanty or scarce.

questions.prompt:
Passage: The library extended its hours during exam week, and students filled every table until closing.

What can be inferred?
questions.explanation: The extended hours and full tables support the inference that students wanted more study time. The other choices contradict or go beyond the text.

questions.prompt: A passage first describes a problem, then lists three possible solutions and their costs. How is the passage organized?
questions.explanation: The passage presents a problem and then discusses solutions, which is problem–solution organization.

nodes.title: Compare & Contrast Passages
nodes.description: Handle paired passages by mapping agreements and disagreements first.
nodes.tip: Build a two-column table for paired passages before answering; shared claims are common answers.

nodes.title: Literary Passages
nodes.description: Read short stories and poems for character, conflict, imagery, and theme.
nodes.tip: Track what changes between the beginning and end; that change usually carries the theme.

nodes.title: Author's Purpose & Tone
nodes.description: Identify why the author writes and how attitude shapes word choice.
nodes.tip: Separate purpose (why) from tone (how it sounds); they are usually two different questions.

nodes.title: Critical Reading & Bias
nodes.description: Evaluate evidence, assumptions, and persuasive framing in an argument.
nodes.tip: Find the unstated assumption: it is the bridge between evidence and conclusion.

nodes.title: Elimination Tactics
nodes.description: Recognize extreme, out-of-scope, and true-but-irrelevant distractors.
nodes.tip: Cross out choices with absolutes (always, never, all) unless the passage states them plainly.

nodes.title: Passage Mapping & Timing
nodes.description: Budget minutes per passage and decide when to move on.
nodes.tip: Cap each passage at its budget; flag one hard question and return only if time remains.

nodes.title: Analysis Exam
nodes.description: Checkpoint covering paired passages, literary passages, author's purpose, critical reading, elimination, and timing.
nodes.tip: Score 80% or higher to master this checkpoint and unlock the advanced group.

questions.prompt:
Passage A argues that school uniforms reduce distractions. Passage B argues that uniforms limit self-expression.

What do both passages agree on?
questions.explanation: Both authors believe uniforms have a meaningful effect on students; they disagree about whether that effect is positive.

questions.prompt:
'The classroom was a zoo after the bell rang.'

Which figure of speech is used?
questions.explanation: The sentence calls the classroom a zoo directly, without using 'like' or 'as,' so it is a metaphor.

questions.prompt: A passage explains how volcanoes form at convergent plate boundaries. What is the author's main purpose?
questions.explanation: The passage explains a scientific process, so its main purpose is to inform.

questions.prompt: A columnist writes: 'Students who read daily score higher, so daily reading raises scores.' Which assumption does the argument rely on?
choices: Reading frequency causes higher scores rather than merely correlating with them.
Students who read daily never watch television.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from a correlation to a causal claim. It assumes that reading is the cause of the higher scores.

questions.prompt: With two minutes left and one passage unchecked, what is the best strategy?
choices: Answer the questions you can and flag the rest instead of reading every line.
Read the passage twice from the beginning.
Spend the remaining time on a finished passage.
questions.explanation: When time is short, secure the answers you can get and flag the rest. Re-reading everything or leaving blanks wastes available points.

nodes.title: Synthesizing Passages
nodes.description: Combine ideas from multiple passages into one accurate, balanced conclusion.
nodes.tip: A synthesis answer must include both passages; an option that mentions only one is usually wrong.

nodes.title: Author's Argument
nodes.description: Identify claims, reasons, evidence, and the logical links that hold an argument together.
nodes.tip: Separate the claim from the evidence; incorrect answers often confuse the two.

nodes.title: Evidence & Support
nodes.description: Judge whether evidence is relevant, sufficient, and actually supports the claim.
nodes.tip: The strongest evidence is specific, relevant, and drawn from a reliable source.

nodes.title: Predicting Answers
nodes.description: Form your own answer before looking at the choices to resist attractive distractors.
nodes.tip: Cover the choices, answer in your own words, then choose the closest match.

nodes.title: Question Order Strategy
nodes.description: Sequence questions from detail to global so earlier answers help with later ones.
nodes.tip: Answer line-reference questions first; they build the map you need for main-idea questions.

nodes.title: Scanning for Details
nodes.description: Find names, dates, numbers, and keywords quickly without re-reading the whole passage.
nodes.tip: Scan with your eyes in a zigzag for the exact keyword, then read the sentence around it.

nodes.title: Strategy & Synthesis Exam
nodes.description: Checkpoint covering synthesis, argument, evidence, prediction, question order, and scanning.
nodes.tip: Score 80% or higher to master this checkpoint and unlock the final simulation.

questions.prompt:
Passage A says remote work raises individual productivity. Passage B says remote work weakens collaboration.

Which statement best synthesizes the two passages?
choices: Remote work can increase individual productivity while weakening collaboration.
Remote work is always better for everyone.
Remote work has no measurable effects.
Both passages reject remote work completely.
questions.explanation: A synthesis combines the main points of both passages without dropping one side. Only the first choice includes both the productivity gain and the collaboration cost.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports the claim that exercise improves mood?
choices: A controlled study finding lower stress scores after regular exercise.
A friend who feels happy after running.
questions.explanation: A controlled study provides systematic, relevant evidence. An anecdote, slogan, or advertisement is much weaker support.

questions.prompt: Why should line-reference questions usually be answered before global questions?
choices: They help you locate details that support broader conclusions.
They are always worth more points.
They require no reading at all.
They are usually the last questions in the section.
questions.explanation: Detail questions force you back into the passage and build a mental map that makes main-idea and inference questions easier.

questions.prompt: To find the year a law was passed in a long passage, what is the fastest approach?
choices: Scan for numerals and the keyword 'law.'
questions.explanation: Scanning targets the exact information you need. Reading every sentence or skipping the passage wastes time or loses accuracy.

questions.prompt: Before reading the answer choices, why predict your own answer?
choices: It reduces the pull of attractive but wrong choices.
It replaces the need to read the passage.
questions.explanation: Predicting first keeps you anchored to the passage's meaning so that a plausible-sounding distractor is easier to reject.

nodes.title: Reading Simulation
nodes.description: Timed multi-passage practice with error analysis.
nodes.tip: Review wrong answers by naming the trap type, not just the correct letter.
